title: The three-quarters exponent and what a biological law has to do
bodyMd:
An animal's resting metabolic rate does not rise in step with its mass. A cow outweighs a rabbit by roughly a hundredfold, yet at rest it consumes far less than a hundred times as much oxygen. In the 1930s a nutritional physiologist proposed that across species metabolic rate rises as mass raised to the three-quarters power, and that exponent has held a privileged place in the discipline ever since. Biology offers few quantitative regularities of such reach, and the three-quarters exponent came to be treated less as a summary of measurements than as a law awaiting a derivation.

A derivation was offered in the late 1990s. Suppose an organism's tissues are served by a branching network — vessels, airways, tracheae — and that three conditions hold: the network reaches every part of the body, it terminates in units whose size does not change with the size of the animal, and its geometry minimizes the energy spent moving material through it. From those premises the three-quarters exponent follows. The model's attraction was never that it fitted the measurements more closely than a curve drawn by hand would have. It was that the model said why the measurements should take that shape at all, and said so from premises about transport rather than premises about metabolism.

The empirical ground has since shifted. As datasets grew larger and were purged of doubtful entries, the estimated exponents stopped clustering tidily. Among birds and among several invertebrate groups the slope sits nearer two-thirds; within a single species, individuals often scale differently than whole species do against one another; and animals measured at maximal exertion do not give the resting exponent. Critics draw the conclusion that the supposed law is a central tendency thrown up by many mechanisms rather than the footprint of one.

Defenders reply that no law in biology is exceptionless and that the departures are noise around a robust average. The reply is fair as far as it goes, but it concedes the very question it must win. If the deviations are unsystematic, they are indeed noise. If instead they track ecology, body plan or stage of development — and some evidence suggests that they do — then the deviations are the phenomenon, and a model that predicts only the average has explained the least interesting part of it. The burden now lies with the network account to say which animals ought to depart from three-quarters, and by how much.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage in comparative physiology. It describes the observation that resting metabolic rate rises more slowly than body mass; the three-quarters-power exponent proposed in the 1930s; a late-1990s model that derives the exponent from assumptions about branching supply networks; empirical findings that estimated exponents vary across taxa, within species and between resting and maximal states; and the author's assessment that the defenders' appeal to noise shifts the burden onto the model to predict the deviations. No figures, tables, equations or mathematical notation appear; the exponents three-quarters and two-thirds are written out in words.

provenance.notes: Written from scratch for this item bank. Not adapted from, and not a paraphrase of, any LSAC passage or any published article. The underlying science (sublinear metabolic scaling, the competing two-thirds and three-quarters exponents, and network-based derivations) is general textbook material; the framing, argument, structure and every sentence are the author's own. No researcher is named and no claim is presented as a citable quotation, precisely so that nothing here reads as a reproduction of a particular source.
